item.title: Looted Goods From French Stores Flood Resale Sites After Riots
item.description:
The online listings started appearing just hours after the looting in France. For sale were a variety of items — handbags, skin care products, lip glosses — suspected of being stolen by people who had smashed windows and emptied stores in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities over the weekend.

Protests in France, which started over conditions in schools and broadened into demonstrations against the rising cost of living, descended into unrest on Saturday and Sunday. Several government buildings were damaged and more than 3,000 shops were looted, leading to the arrest of more than 2,500 people, officials said.

In Paris, many of the shops across Les Halles were looted and vandalized, while the Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde became center points for standoffs between the police and protesters. Stores that were broken into included Louis Vuitton, Céline, Hermès and the North Face, as well as video game shops, pharmacies and electronics stores. A preliminary estimate showed the damage would cost several hundred million euros.

Resale sites like Vinted said this week that they were cracking down on items suspected to have been looted. Vinted said it was working with the French authorities to detect malicious behavior.

“Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings,” Vinted said in a statement. “When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans.”

President Emmanuel Macron of France warned on Sunday that “those who looted will have to pay back, and those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable.”

But many more people participated in the looting than the police will be able to arrest, and it will be virtually impossible for resale sites to take down all stolen items because of the scale of the theft, said Charlotte de Montpellier, an economist at ING Bank.

“I don’t expect that those companies will be able to track everything,” she said. The test for the broader French economy, she added, will be how long the protests last, and whether the unrest continues. “More could come, and that will of course have a significant impact on the final bill,” she said.

France was calm on Wednesday, but Sébastien Lecornu, the prime minister, said a significant security operation was planned ahead of more protests expected on Saturday.

Serge Papin, the trade minister, and Anne Le Hénanff, the digital affairs minister, met on Monday with resale platforms to discuss strengthening their cooperation with the French authorities to identify and report stolen goods. Alliance Française des Places de Marché, which represents platforms like eBay, Vinted and Etsy, said in a statement after the meeting that its members had agreed to increase monitoring to detect goods that might have been obtained through looting and inform consumers of the penalties associated with buying stolen goods.

The damage to companies goes beyond replacing looted products. On Tuesday, Carrefour, the largest food retailer in France, lowered its full-year financial targets because of indirect costs of the riots: increased spending on security and logistics, fewer customers, precautionary closures and reduced hours because of curfews.

“Our group is facing an unprecedented situation in France,” Alexandre Bompard, the company’s chief executive, said in a statement. “There is a high degree of uncertainty regarding consumer spending trends and the conditions under which our stores will be able to open.” He said about 50 stores had been affected by vandals, costing the company at least tens of millions of euros.

The French government said businesses that had been forced to reduce or suspend their activity after the damage could get financial assistance like interest-free loans. Employees who are unable to work would receive compensation equal to 60 percent of their salaries, and those earning minimum wage would receive their full paychecks. Businesses could also apply for emergency grants of up to €1,500, or about $1,700, and the government is establishing a support fund for businesses with fewer than 50 employees, which will be able to receive a lump-sum payment.

If riots continue, the concern is that tourists will cancel trips to Paris and that business owners may feel reluctant to start new businesses or reopen shops, Ms. de Montpellier said. For these reasons, “we think that it may have a slightly bigger impact” on the economy than the major protests in France in 2018, she said.

item.title: When Do Rules on Historic Preservation Go Too Far?
item.description:
When Jillian and Dan Massetti discovered last year that the slate roof on their 140-year-old house was leaking, they considered replacing it with a composite material resembling slate that would have cost them $45,000. But because the house is in a historic district in Saratoga Springs, N.Y., the couple needed the approval of the city’s Design Review Board.

After four appearances, the board narrowly ruled that because of the house’s prominent location, the Massettis had to use real slate. The cost: $115,000.

When the couple protested, one board member told them: “You bought into the district. You didn’t do your research on it.”

Ms. Massetti told The New York Times she loved living in a historic part of the city and was eager to preserve her home. But she worried that a new slate roof would be too costly.

The ruling generated some criticism from the city’s Republican mayor, John Safford, and the board later agreed to reverse it. But as Ms. Massetti said during a City Council hearing this month, “Homeowners should not have to reach a crisis point before common sense enters the process.”

The debate in Saratoga Springs takes place at a time when more places have embraced the preservation movement partly in hopes of boosting tourism and increasing property values. In the New York town, the dispute underscores the huge role that the movement has come to play and how its efforts have transformed the local economy. Millions of visitors come to the city each year to savor its charm and character and take in its meticulously preserved Victorian architecture.

But the desire to preserve the past has also touched off fierce debates in cities like Bisbee, Ariz., and Cape May, N.J., about the future, especially when many municipalities face a severe housing shortage.

Ted Grevstad-Nordbrock, an associate professor of urban planning and development at Iowa State University, calls himself a “dyed-in-the-wool preservationist,” but says neighborhoods that are anointed as historic can accelerate gentrification and lead to long-term changes in race and income.

In Saratoga Springs, Mr. Safford has proposed changes that would relax the city’s preservation rules, including allowing property owners to be able to appeal rulings by the Design Review Board in order to make projects more financially feasible.

As Mr. Safford sees it, preservation has done the city a lot of good. But its strict design standards have also made it harder for a lot of people to maintain and renovate their homes. Homeowners in these districts who want to replace windows or remove a dilapidated porch, for example, must first get approval from the Design Review Board, whose seven members, usually with a design background or interest, are appointed by the mayor.

Mr. Safford said there was a risk that the city’s exacting design standards would put large parts of the city out of reach for anyone but the well-heeled. “We’ll just have tourists and wealthy people here.”

Business owners will also have a hard time, he said. For example, in 2023 the convenience store chain Stewart’s Shops announced plans to expand one of its stores by tearing down a 145-year-old house next door, leading to a bitter three-year court battle. It was resolved this year, when a judge ruled that the building could come down but that the review board would get to approve the new design.

Tamie Ehinger, chair of the board, said its goal was to ensure that any exterior design changes “are compatible and appropriate for the particular district.”

The mayor’s proposed changes, which still must be approved by the City Council, have generated heated debate in recent months. Samantha Bosshart, executive director of the Saratoga Springs Preservation Foundation, once called them “probably the biggest threat to preservation in decades here.”

Amid the pressure, the mayor has backed away from some ideas, such as a proposal to allow the City Council to have final say about whether a building could be demolished in the so-called Architectural Review District.

More than 2,100 cities and towns, including at least 70 in New York State, participate in the Certified Local Government program, jointly administered by the National Park Service and individual State Historic Preservation Offices, which helps communities set preservation standards. They include a growing number of places known for midcentury modern architecture. A historic designation makes them eligible for tax credits in some states, said Chris Cody, associate general counsel for the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Among them is New York, which allows homeowners who renovate properties in some historic neighborhoods in the state to defray part of the cost.

Saratoga Springs is seen as a success story and has won multiple awards for its efforts from the American Public Works Association and the Preservation League of New York State. Travel and Leisure magazine named the city’s Broadway one of “America’s Greatest Main Streets.”

Starting in the 1970s, city officials set about fixing a town that had grown shabby. Many of the city’s historic buildings had fallen into disrepair. The main drag, Broadway, was pockmarked with empty storefronts. Magnificent old hotels like the Grand Union were torn down. The city established two historic districts, where decisions about renovation and building demolition are tightly controlled.

Saratoga Springs went from a place that had long seen its population mushroom in the summer, when its famed horse racing track opens and the Philadelphia Orchestra comes to town, to a year-round destination, said Ms. Bosshart of the Saratoga Springs Preservation Foundation. Its motto today is “health, history and horses.”

“Preservation has been a key to our city’s success,” she said. “It’s made us a destination. It’s made us a desirable place to live.”

One recent afternoon, Ms. Ehinger, the design board chair, drove through town, pointing out some of the city’s prized buildings. There were tidy brick rowhouses that date to the 1860s, and elaborate clapboard-sided mansions with columned porticos, stained-glass windows and wide porches. And there was the stately Adelphi, the last of the elaborate hotels where visitors once stayed when they came to bathe in the mineral springs.

At one point, she stopped in front of a new house. The owners had torn down an older home and replaced it with one far taller than its neighbors, with a jarring patchwork of design materials that horrified neighbors, she said. But the lot was outside the historic district, so the city had exerted little control over the building’s design. This is what happens without design standards, she said.

“Many people owned the property before you, and many people will own it after you,” she said. “Your time as an owner, you’re really a steward for the property. It’s important that changes you make are done appropriately.”

Critics of the preservation movement say its efforts have contributed to the country’s housing shortage, but how much is a subject of debate. Housing prices soared across the country during the Covid pandemic, not just in Saratoga Springs.

North Broadway is lined with stately old mansions that now sell for upward of $8 million.

Those kinds of prices are far from typical. Still, the median housing price has risen 63 percent since 2018 to $656,614 today, according to Zillow. And Mr. Safford warns that rising costs make it harder for younger, “more entrepreneurial” people to live in Saratoga Springs.

“They’re the ones that keep the lifeblood of the city moving, and we’re basically telling them they can’t live here anymore because they can’t afford the historical standards,” he said.

But despite rising construction costs, building continues in Saratoga Springs, which issues more building permits than any other place in the Albany metro area, said Jay DiLorenzo, president of the Preservation League of New York State.

Ms. Ehinger concedes that the city needs to strike a balance between preserving the past and preparing for the future. That means making accommodations with developers and homeowners when possible. Not every old building is worth saving, she said.

“New development is vital; towns need to grow,” Ms. Ehinger said. “But it needs to be done in a smart manner so that it doesn’t compromise the integrity of the historic district.”

item.title: For Clues About How A.I. Will Change Work, Look to the Past
item.description:
In December 1931, economists gathered in Washington to discuss the threat that technology posed to American workers.

Switchboard operators were being rendered obsolete by the dial telephone. Movie-theater musicians were superfluous in the age of “talkies.” Teamsters — men driving teams of horses — were losing their jobs to drivers of gasoline-powered trucks.

Such disruptions were nothing new, the economists conceded. But with the Great Depression raging, the risks to the economy and social stability seemed greater than ever. And it was all happening “more rapidly than in any previous age,” warned Sumner H. Slichter, a Harvard economist.

“And yet we have failed, for the most part, to recognize that change presents a major social problem,” he told colleagues at the annual meeting of the American Economic Association.

Nearly a century later, a new generation of economists is trying to make sense of the consequences of another technology: artificial intelligence. And while the jobs they are focused on are different — computer programmers instead of telephone operators, scriptwriters instead of movie musicians, drivers of trucks powered by diesel, not animals — many of the questions they are asking are the same.

Would the undeniable benefits of technology be enjoyed broadly, or accrue only to the wealthy few? Would new jobs emerge in time to replace the ones being destroyed? Was government data up to the task of measuring the rapidly changing economy? And, most importantly, what could the government do to slow these disruptions, or at least to help the workers caught in their wake?

“Technological changes may be so rapid and so far-reaching that they bring about a condition in which all factors of production may be simultaneously unemployed,” Ewan Clague, an economist who later served as commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, told colleagues in 1931. He even proposed a policy that would not seem out of place in today’s A.I. debate: “Might it not be possible to work out a method of taxing machinery and equipment which would tend to slow down their development?”

Modern economists are revisiting these earlier eras to find lessons relevant to policymakers today. Why did mechanization in the textile industry create widespread unemployment among spinners but not among weavers? Why were the protests that workers staged against industrialization in the 19th century more violent in France than in England? (And why did other technological changes draw little protest at all?)

Why, in short, have some episodes of technological upheaval gone relatively well for workers, and others so badly?

Historical examples are particularly useful right now, economists argue, because this moment is so uncertain. The models that economists typically rely on offer an almost comically broad range of potential outcomes, from a modest productivity boost on a par with that of the internet to “an unprecedented transformation of our economy, larger than the Industrial Revolution, but unfolding over a vastly shorter time frame,” as nearly 200 economists warned in a recent letter.

History won’t provide a definitive answer, said Ben Schneider, an economist at the University of Oslo who studies how technology affects workers. But it can offer a window into the way societies have handled previous periods of rapid change.

“We can look to the past and we can say, well, the implications of the steam engine have basically played out by now,” Mr. Schneider said.

When the economists met in Washington in 1931, unemployment was nearly 20 percent, and would hit 25 percent within a year, which remains a record.

Worries about technology’s taking jobs predated the Depression, but the crisis made them more acute. When telephone companies began replacing manual switchboards with dial telephones in the 1920s, tens of thousands of jobs disappeared. But most of the displaced workers — overwhelmingly young women — found other jobs relatively quickly.

“During the period of business expansion before 1929, technological displacement led directly to relatively little unemployment,” economists at the Bureau of Labor Statistics wrote in a 1932 report, “The Dial Telephone and Unemployment.”

The Depression changed everything. Women who lost their jobs connecting calls had little hope of finding work elsewhere. There were similar challenges in manufacturing, where automation allowed factories to produce steel, car parts and other goods with far fewer workers.

“How empty a modern steel mill seems!” The New York Times Magazine lamented in 1938. “There is something ominous about this — ominous because of the short cuts to come.”

A few years later, however, those mills were producing steel for the American war effort, and with men off fighting, labor-saving technology was a boon rather than a threat. And in the economic boom in the decades after World War II, concerns about technological displacement were mitigated by the abundant job opportunities — many of them tied to designing, manufacturing and selling cars, televisions and washing machines for a growing middle class — that ensured that many displaced workers could find new jobs relatively quickly.

A century earlier, the same pattern had played out in reverse, with much worse outcomes for workers. Landowners in England adopted threshing machines to fill in for scarce human labor when agricultural workers were off fighting Napoleon. When men returned from war, they found that a critical source of work — threshing accounted for as much as half of a rural laborer’s income during the winter months — had evaporated.

What followed were the “Swing Riots,” a wave of unrest in 1830s England that surpassed the better-known protests of the Luddites.

The state of the broader economy, in other words, plays a critical role in deciding how workers will fare when technology disrupts their livelihoods. Timing matters. So does geography — it’s better to lose a job in a region that is thriving than in one that is struggling.

Violent protests against the adoption of threshing machines were much more common in remote areas, said Bruno Caprettini, an economist who has studied the uprising. Closer to cities, where workers could seek other employment, protests were less intense. And by the mid-19th century, as the economy improved and wages rose, protests died down as workers found better-paying jobs.

“Nobody misses manual threshing,” Mr. Caprettini said. What they missed was the stability that threshing provided. If workers have other opportunities, they will adapt. If they don’t, they will protest, or even revolt.

One reason workers were hit so hard by automation during the first Industrial Revolution and in the 1930s is that their jobs disappeared so quickly — literally overnight in the case of telephone operators. Phone companies typically made the transition from manual to mechanized dialing at midnight on a Saturday, when call volumes were low. Operators who had jobs when they went home on Friday were out of work by Monday morning.

Such rapid changes gave workers little time to adapt. Not only were women who lost their jobs as telephone operators less likely to be working in the telephone industry a decade later, they were less likely to be working at all, according to a 2024 study. And those who did have jobs tended to earn lower wages than before the switch to dial phones.

In industries where the transitions were more gradual, workers tended to fare better.

By the time gasoline-powered passenger cars became prevalent in the 1900s, for example, it was clear that the technology would eventually come for delivery trucks. But it was only after World War I that motor trucks displaced horse-drawn wagons en masse. The number of teamsters actually rose from 1900 to 1910, then declined gradually in the 1910s before dropping precipitously in the 1920s and ’30s.

The relatively slow transition allowed young men, recognizing there was no future in driving horses, to pursue other industries. That left a shortage of drivers, which meant that wages actually rose for the mostly older workers who stuck around to finish out their careers.

Something similar may be happening today as modern drivers face a new technological disruption: self-driving trucks. That threat, too, has been clear for years, and there are signs that younger workers have become more reluctant to enter the industry, said Kevin Lang, an economist at Boston University.

But while truckers have had some warning, A.I. appears to be threatening jobs that until recently seemed relatively safe from technological upheaval, such as software development and legal services. That, too, has echoes of the 1930s, said Amy Bix, a historian at Iowa State University.

“There really was a deep set of concerns in the Depression era that technology was advancing faster than society’s ability to adjust, and that people were sort of being left to fend for themselves in the wreckage,” she said. “Today, you really do have a very similar sense of uncertainty and fear that these technological changes are all coming so rapidly.”

The A.I. debate, like earlier episodes of technological change, tends to focus on the threat of job losses. But economists say the true impact is often subtler. Technology sometimes costs jobs, they say, but it almost always changes them.

In 1851, about 220,000 people worked as boot makers in England. The number hardly changed over the next six decades, rising and falling only modestly before settling at about 207,000 in 1911.

“If you look just at that, you might think, OK, not that much has happened in this industry,” said Hillary Vipond, an economic historian.

In fact, the industry changed entirely over that period. The boot makers of the mid-19th century were artisans, working in towns throughout England. The boot makers of the early-20th century were factory workers in cities, producing far more boots per hour at far lower prices than their artisan predecessors.

The episode carries several lessons, Ms. Vipond said. Technology made workers more productive, but that didn’t result in a loss of jobs, because lower prices led to increased demand — a phenomenon known as “Jevon’s paradox.” More people could afford boots; owners of one pair could now buy several.

But while the number of jobs didn’t fall, the work changed. That is what often gets missed in discussions of technological disruption, Ms. Vipond said: Technologies destroy jobs, but they also create new ones. By one estimate, roughly 60 percent of jobs in the United States in 2018 were in occupations that didn’t exist in 1940.

“We don’t focus enough on the new jobs,” she said. “The reason this hasn’t been a crisis before is because in every decade we have seen new jobs emerge.”

Still, Ms. Vipond said, just because new jobs eventually emerge doesn’t mean that transitions are easy for workers. The Industrial Revolution displaced so many workers so rapidly that it crushed wages for decades — a period known as “Engel’s Pause” — before demand caught up with supply and workers’ living standards began improving again.

Even shorter disruptions can be painful for the workers caught in the crossfire, said Mr. Schneider, the University of Oslo economist. Losing a job and being unemployed is costly for workers and their families, even if they eventually find another.

“It’s easy for us today to look back and say, yeah, there was some disruption, but basically, in the end, it was worth it,” Mr. Schneider said. “And maybe for us it was worth it. But for the people at the time, it might not have felt like it was worth it for them.”

Most economists don’t give much credence to predictions that A.I. will mean the end of work. But the disruptions it causes could dwarf past episodes. The A.I. revolution is also global, affecting not just the rich economies where the technology is being developed, but also poorer countries that have built their economies partly on call centers, tech support and other back-office industries that could be vulnerable to technological upheaval.

Mr. Lang, the Boston University economist, said that if A.I. wipes out a large share of white-collar jobs, it isn’t clear what would replace them.

“I have colleagues who say we’ve been worried the world is going to collapse many times in the past, and it never has,” Mr. Lang said. “To which my response is, I’ve been sick many times, but I’ve never died.”

item.title: Employers Shift Rising Health Care Costs Onto Millions of Workers
item.description:
Working families are paying much more for health insurance this year, with many postponing doctor’s visits, treatments or filling prescriptions. The number of uninsured Americans is rising as more people wrestle with unpaid medical bills.

This is the stark picture emerging from two surveys released Thursday that show how millions of people in the United States are struggling to keep up with sharply climbing medical costs in recent years.

As the midterm elections approach, Americans are ranking health care near or at the top of their financial concerns, according to a recent poll from KFF, a nonprofit health research group.

Roughly six in 10 adults reported they were very or somewhat worried about affording care.

The majority of Americans — about 157 million — get insurance through their employer. But as costs for coverage have spiked, with increases in the high single digits, businesses have been shifting much more of the additional expenses onto their workforces.

Employees are paying more for coverage, especially if they work for a small business, according to KFF, which released its an annual survey of employers about their health benefits.

Many people are also paying thousands of dollars in medical expenses when they get sick, because companies have increased the plans’ deductibles to offset increases in premiums.

The yearly price, on average, for employees to cover their family is now $7,471 a year, up 9 percent from 2025. The total cost for a family plan, including the amount the employer contributes to the annual premiums, has reached $28,303.

Overall, the average deductible for U.S. workers is approaching $2,000 before insurance kicks in, according to the survey.

“People tell us in polls that their health care costs are their top cost-of-living concern, tied with gas prices. The fact that workers’ share of premiums went up almost three times faster than inflation in 2026 helps explain why,” said Drew Altman, the president and chief executive of KFF, in an email.

Harder hit are employees of small companies, defined as those with fewer than 200 workers, whose paychecks have been shrinking as premiums increase, according to the KFF survey. On average, they are paying $9,687 a year for coverage.

More than a third of people working at a small employer have annual deductibles of $3,000 or more.

Companies are also erecting new hurdles for workers to get care, like cumbersome approval processes for expensive drugs or treatments, the KFF survey found. Another way that businesses are trying to lower costs has been to restrict employees’ choices of doctors or hospitals.

“Employers are paying the equivalent of buying an economy car for each employee who has family health insurance coverage, and in 2026 they offloaded more of that cost to workers,” Mr. Altman said. KFF surveyed more than 1,900 employers with at least 10 workers.

For their part, employers attribute higher costs to several factors, including hospital care, expensive new cancer therapies and expanding coverage of GLP-1 medications for obesity and diabetes.

The rollbacks in government programs like Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act have also left more people without health coverage, according to a separate survey from the Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit research foundation that analyzes Americans’ experience with insurance every other year. The fund has been a longtime supporter of the A.C.A. and other efforts to expand coverage.

The share of working-age adults who are uninsured rose to 11.2 percent in 2026 from 8.9 percent in 2024, the Commonwealth study showed. Conducted from early May through mid-July, the study has provided one of the first indications of whether people no longer enrolled in Medicaid and Obamacare found other sources of insurance.

The increase in the uninsured rate over the last two years “was really notable,” said Sara R. Collins, a senior scholar at the fund who led the Commonwealth research.

After Obamacare was enacted in 2010, the number of working-age adults and children without insurance fell from around 46 million to a low of about 25 million three years ago. The government changes and soaring medical costs across the broader health sector have fueled a backslide in coverage, bringing the estimated number this year to 30 million uninsured, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

The Trump administration is expected to release official figures on the number of uninsured Americans next year.

The recent increase is statistically significant, Ms. Collins said, and the previous Commonwealth estimates of the uninsured rate have been lower than the official government figures and generally tracked in the same direction.

The Commonwealth survey also noted that about 12 percent of working-age adults reported a gap or lapse in their insurance, the same share as in 2022.

The increase in the uninsured rate was not unexpected, with some estimates showing that nearly five million people dropped their individual coverage. Many were no longer able to afford their Obamacare insurance after President Trump and Republican lawmakers declined to extend pandemic-era subsidies that had helped defray the cost of a typical plan.

Enrollment in Medicaid, the federal-state program for the poor, has also been declining, although the bulk of the cuts to that program as part of Mr. Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act do not take place until next year. Over the last four years, the share of working-age adults enrolled in Medicaid dropped from 15.5 percent to 13 percent, according to Commonwealth.

But the Commonwealth survey, which was based on telephone and online interviews among a sample of 9,360 adults, also underscored how financially insecure people have become about their ability to pay for medical care. The number of people who said they had delayed or skipped care altogether because of the expense increased to 50 percent this year from 46 percent in 2022, according to the survey.

“These reports show the reason why health care costs are at the top of voter concern and outrage,” said Anthony Wright, the executive director of Families USA, a left-leaning consumer advocacy group.

The deepening strains on household budgets are also evident as the rate of medical debt or unpaid bills keeps rising, affecting even those who are insured. About a third of adults with individual policies and those with coverage from an employer reported they were paying off medical bills or medical debt they had already incurred, according to the Commonwealth Fund.

People without insurance tend to have lower levels of medical debt, Ms. Collins of Commonwealth said. “You just use less care if you don’t have insurance coverage.”

The survey found that most Americans believed the federal government had a responsibility to ensure that people had coverage, although Democrats and independents expressed that belief more strongly than Republicans.

“They are mad at hospitals and drug companies and insurers for charging so much,” said Mr. Wright of Families USA. “They are furious at Congress for not reining them in.”

Employers and insurers “have never addressed, not in a significant way, the drivers of health care costs,” Ms. Collins said. “Health care costs are the thing that drives premiums and deductibles.”

item.title: Stocks Fall and Oil Rises as Investors Retreat from Mounting Risks
item.description:
Global markets shuddered on Thursday as stocks fell after earnings reports from big technology companies spooked investors and oil jumped to its highest level in months on a series of worrisome developments in the conflict in the Middle East.

Strikes in Saudi Arabia and around the Persian Gulf helped drive the price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, up 3 percent to about $112 a barrel, its highest level since May.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, also rose, to nearly $100 a barrel.

Oil had reached as high as $120 a barrel since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran nearly eight months ago, which has disrupted exports from the energy-rich Persian Gulf region. Before the war, global oil was trading around $70 a barrel and about 20 percent of the world’s oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz, an artery between Iran and Oman that has become treacherous for commercial ships since the start of the fighting. Oil flows through the strait are running at about 75 percent of prewar levels, according to Kpler, a maritime data company.

In the United States, the average price of gasoline was $4.27 a gallon on Thursday, according to the AAA motor club, up 43 percent since the war began. The average price of diesel has surged 68 percent over that period, to $6.31 per gallon.

Notes: Data shows future contract prices for Brent crude oil. Gaps indicate nontrading hours. Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Futures on the S&P 500 pointed to a 1 percent decline when stocks resume trading in the United States on Thursday. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was set for a steeper fall, approaching 2 percent.

Large tech companies at the forefront of the A.I. expansion pulled down market indexes, as investors have grown more wary of the returns promised by wildly expensive A.I. projects. On Wednesday after markets closed, Meta reported a big decline in its cash flow and said it would issue a new class of stock to help raise more money to spend on data centers and other A.I. initiatives. Earnings at Tesla fell short of Wall Street expectations, as the automaker run by Elon Musk poured resources into self-driving vehicles, humanoid robots and other new technologies.

Major markets in Asia, which are heavily influenced by technology industry trends, posted declines, with benchmark indexes in Hong Kong, Japan and South Korea all down by at least 2 percent. In Europe, the Stoxx 600, an index that tracks the region’s largest companies, fell about 1 percent.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Violence flared in the Middle East overnight, another factor weighing on markets. At least two people were killed in a strike on an airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, the home city of Saudi Aramco, the state oil giant. Two other people died after air defenses intercepted a drone that targeted an oil field run by Aramco. The Saudi government did not say who they believed was responsible for the attacks. The Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen has been striking Saudi infrastructure for weeks.

Saudi Aramco staff were instructed to leave the company’s headquarters building in Dhahran and to work remotely on Thursday, according to two people familiar with the situation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak for the company. Aramco did not respond to a request for comment and the Saudi energy ministry referred questions to Aramco.

In the Persian Gulf, several commercial ships have been attacked in recent days. On Tuesday night, a tanker carrying oil products, the Soyia, was reportedly struck while at anchor in the northern Persian Gulf, according to Marisks, a maritime risk firm. Another ship, a Kuwait-flagged crude oil tanker, was struck on Wednesday while sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire on the ship, according to a maritime agency operated by Pakistan’s Navy.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said on Thursday that it had struck four tankers in the northern Persian Gulf that it claimed had been illegally transferring oil. It also said that three more vessels had hit mines in the western Strait of Hormuz. Those attacks could not immediately be independently confirmed.

In an article published in The Financial Times, Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister, said that Iran, “simply by virtue of geography, will always have unparalleled leverage over maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.” He warned that any further escalation from the United States would result in a “painful outcome.”

Jenny Gross and Lisa Friedman contributed reporting from London.

item.title: Zuckerberg’s Big Deal
item.description:
Andrew here. A quick note: For those of you hoping to join us at this year’s DealBook Summit on Nov. 18, we are going to be closing applications shortly given the overwhelming interest.

We have a huge day of interviews planned, including with Vice President JD Vance, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla, David Ellison of Skydance, Hailey Bieber of Rhode, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York and Christine Lagarde of the European Central Bank, among others. (Check out the full list.) Apply here to attend in person.

Meta stunned investors with its quarterly earnings report, including soaring revenue and spending on artificial intelligence. (More on that below.)

But the most eye-grabbing news was the deal that Mark Zuckerberg, the company’s billionaire C.E.O., negotiated with his own board to stay in California.

It was the most public sign yet of how companies are grappling with the risk of a potential tax on many of the state’s billionaires.

How it went down:

Zuckerberg had been negotiating with Meta’s board since July over how the company would help him deal with the proposed billionaire tax, according to a regulatory filing. He was aiming to establish residency outside California before the vote on the measure next month.

Zuckerberg wanted a new class of nonvoting stock that he could sell to pay for any tax liability he would incur if voters approved the proposal.

On Sept. 9, he told board members that he would list his home in Palo Alto for sale on Sept. 13 if they didn’t reach an agreement. That was seen as both a potential P.R. disaster and a possible blow to the company’s A.I. work.

Meta quickly hammered out a deal, creating new Class C shares. Zuckerberg can immediately sell up to 20 percent of his stock, or about 10 percent of his financial stake in the company, “for any reason.”

In return, Zuckerberg agreed to reside in California for eight more years, except under some conditions.

The problem Zuckerberg faced: While his net worth is estimated at $247 billion, his actual wealth is far less liquid. He estimated that he would have to sell some of his “supervoting” shares to pay his tax liability, which The Times estimated could be nearly $12.5 billion. That could take his voting power down to 53 percent from about 60 percent.

The new shares allow him to raise billions from stock sales without weakening his grip on the company.

They also let Meta raise more money for its huge A.I. investment ambitions, in addition to the billions it has borrowed over the past two years. Investors told DealBook’s Niko Gallogly that they wouldn’t be surprised if the company did so before Anthropic’s I.P.O., which is expected as soon as next month.

What are other tech companies doing? Meta’s move underscores the fears tech executives have about the California tax. Dozens of moguls, including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin and several Meta board members, have donated millions to fight the proposal.

Yet the measure’s outlook remains uncertain. Polling suggests that support for it has fallen in recent months, and the odds of its passage implied by trading on Kalshi and Polymarket are under 25 percent.

Oil prices surge. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, briefly traded above $112 on Thursday on fears that the war with Iran could escalate. The Times reports that the U.S. and Israel are drawing up plans for new strikes on the country after the American midterm elections. There were deadly incidents at an airport in Saudi Arabia and around a Saudi Aramco oil field, amid the war between the kingdom and the Iran-backed Houthi militia. (There were no immediate claims of responsibility.) Elsewhere, Peter Thiel, the tech mogul and Republican donor, told attendees at a private event this month that Washington “should not have” gone to war with Tehran, according to Politico, which obtained audio from the event. “I’m skeptical,” he added.

The F.C.C. chair threatens news outlets over polls. The agency’s head, Brendan Carr, warned that news media outlets could be punished for publishing what the Trump administration deemed inaccurate election polling results — as a new poll showed President Trump‘s approval rating hitting a record low. The push is the latest example of Carr threatening outlets Trump considers critical of him.

Goldman Sachs introduces an A.I. initiative for small businesses. The Wall Street giant announced that the Goldman Sachs Small Business AI Institute, a program aimed at providing educational and technological resources for smaller companies, was partnering with Anthropic, Google, Meta and OpenAI. It’s part of a $500 million expansion of Goldman’s 10,000 Small Businesses program, and is the latest sign of companies’ making A.I. a focus of their philanthropy.

The artificial intelligence stock rally is under pressure again as spending concerns weigh on investors. That includes Meta, the first hyperscaler to report this earnings season.

Shares of the company are falling in premarket trading after Meta reported record quarterly revenue. The tech giant also disclosed a steep increase in spending that is pressuring its finances, Niko Gallogly reports.

The latest:

Nasdaq Composite futures are down 1.7 percent.

South Korea’s Kospi index, a bellwether for A.I. stocks, also fell.

DeepSeek, the fast-growing Chinese chatbot maker, raised about $15 billion in new funds, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed sources.

Meta had a breakthrough quarter for A.I. Executives said its Muse agent has had more than 10 million downloads since its introduction last month. They added that the company planned to build infrastructure to serve more than a billion Muse users over the next few years.

That comes at a steep price. While Meta announced a 26 percent year-on-year jump in quarterly revenue to $64.6 billion, total expenses soared 68 percent to $51.6 billion.

The company now expects to spend $135 billion to $145 billion in capital expenditures this fiscal year, higher than a previous outlook of $130 billion to $145 billion. To offset its steep spending, “we are going to work on monetization somewhat sooner on this than our normal playbook,” Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s C.E.O., told analysts on Wednesday.

Meta has been borrowing heavily to finance that spending spree. It issued $30 billion of corporate bonds in October 2025, and another $25 billion this April.

The overall A.I. borrowing surge has given the credit market “indigestion,” Michael Haber, a credit strategist at Jefferies told DealBook. It has pushed up borrowing costs on A.I.-related corporate debt, including Meta’s.

The tech giant faces another financial hit. Hours before its earnings call, a judge in New Mexico ordered it to pay a $25 billion penalty for privacy practices considered deceptive.

That’s in addition to Meta’s agreement to pay up to $17 billion to settle a broad lawsuit with other states over child safety and make significant changes to its products.

Watch Tesla, too. The electric vehicle maker reported a net profit on Wednesday that missed analysts’ expectations, and cut its spending forecast.

In a call with analysts, Elon Musk declined to elaborate on whether he would ultimately combine Tesla with SpaceX.

Number of the day

That’s the total annual cost for an employer-administered family health insurance plan, Reed Abelson reports for The Times. (That’s an increase of roughly 5 percent from 2025.) Of that, employees pay an average of $7,471 a year. The figures come from KFF, a nonprofit health research group that releases an annual employer health benefits survey.

Companies and government agencies are still scrambling to patch a major software security vulnerability that could put large parts of the web at risk.

The race to stop hackers from exploiting the vulnerabilities led organizations around the globe to take offline some of their internet services as they gauged the cost of patching the weaknesses and potential liabilities they faced if they failed to do so, Sri Muppidi and Bernhard Warner report.

What happened? Researchers found and disclosed security vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language that is key internet architecture. They recommended that users patch the issues. By some estimates, the software is used by approximately 70 percent of all websites and web applications.

That set off alarms. The National Security Agency’s cybersecurity unit on Wednesday advised organizations that couldn’t patch the flaws immediately to take down their systems. Some European governments, Wikipedia and companies were affected. That included the Asahi Group and the airline ANA in Japan, The Financial Times reported. A slew of other outages were visible on Downdetector on Wednesday. (A separate Google Cloud outage may have added to the wider disruption.)

A.I. wore the “white hat” this time. Researchers at security firm Calif detected the bugs, known as PHP2Shell, using OpenAI’s advanced artificial intelligence models; Wiz, a security company owned by Google, also independently identified them.

But hackers could also use A.I. to try to exploit the issue. Until a website operator applies the patches, it’s vulnerable to an attack, Vyas Sekar, a professor at Carnegie Mellon University who is affiliated with its security institute CyLab, told DealBook.

It’s unclear what the eventual cost of the disruption may be. Those who don’t fix the flaw could face potential liabilities if their sites are hacked, analysts say.

“The websites that went offline today may be the ones we should worry about least,” Mikko Hypponen, a Finnish cybersecurity expert, told DealBook. “They are the ones that are getting patched.”

Security experts are on high alert. Amazon Threat Intelligence, part of the tech giant’s cloud division, wrote in a blog post on Wednesday that it had identified what appeared to be an attempt to exploit PHP2Shell four days before it was disclosed to the public.

Matthew Prince, the C.E.O. of the cybersecurity firm Cloudflare, wrote on social media that Cloudflare had recorded thousands of attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities in the 10 hours leading up to the disclosure.

Deals

Mathias Döpfner, the C.E.O. of the media giant Axel Springer, reportedly pitched a deal to buy a stake in TikTok’s European operations to Charles Kushner, the U.S. ambassador to France. (FT)

Blackstone and Apollo Global Management are said to be in talks with the N.F.L. to win approval to buy minority stakes in the league’s teams. (Bloomberg)

“It Looks Like a Music Festival. It’s Really a Sales Pitch for Private Credit.” (WSJ)

Politics, policy and regulation

President Trump announced a whistle-blower incentive program to combat fraud, but skeptics are worried that he could use it for political purposes. (NYT)

New Mexico sued a lawyer and an accountant of Jeffrey Epstein, accusing them of helping finance and conceal sex trafficking at a ranch the disgraced financier owned in the state. (WSJ)

Best of the rest

Is “tradwife” social media content hurting women in the workplace? Sheryl Sandberg thinks so. (Fortune)

“In France, Raging Against the Luxury Machine” (NYT)

What’s behind the boom in gray paint? Data centers. (NYT)

We’d like your feedback! Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.title: Barclays to Cut 5,000 Jobs in A.I.-Driven Push to Lower Costs
item.description:
Barclays said Thursday that it would cut about 5,000 jobs as the British bank and its competitors rely more heavily on artificial intelligence to increase efficiency and lower costs.

The company, based in London, is the latest to announce job cuts linked to its use of artificial intelligence. Standard Chartered set off a debate in May when it said it would eliminate more than 7,000 jobs.

The layoffs at Barclays, which account for 5 percent of the bank’s work force, come as investors and economists look for evidence that A.I. can deliver on its promise to raise profits and productivity. Anxiety is widespread that the technology could lead to job losses in banking, law and similar fields. Britain has a large finance industry and is seen as particularly exposed to disruption by artificial intelligence.

About 60 percent of the job cuts at Barclays will affect employees with support roles, including software developers, the company said in a presentation on Thursday after reporting a 12 percent increase in quarterly profit that fell short of what analysts had forecast. Barclays cited “organizational simplification and technology change efficiency” from its use of artificial intelligence.

“A.I. has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” C.S. Venkatakrishnan, the chief executive of Barclays, told reporters on a call. The company plans to employ A.I. “at scale,” but he added that A.I. is “the icing on the cake, not the cake.”

In May, Bill Winters, the head of London-based Standard Chartered, sought to reassure employees after the lender announced plans to cut thousands of support jobs over four years. Mr. Winter raised an outcry in describing the cuts as “replacing in some cases lower-value human capital with the financial capital and the investment capital we’re putting in.”

In the United States, artificial intelligence is the main reason cited by employers to reduce their work forces, with A.I. highlighted by companies more than 120,000 times this year, or more than a fifth of all the cuts announced, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas, a research firm.

Barclays, which expects its efficiency measures to deliver savings of more than 1.1 billion pounds, or $1.5 billion, next year, said it had already cut 1,000 of the roles. The company added in a statement that it was “building the work force and skills needed to deliver our strategy and meet the evolving needs of our customers and clients.”

item.title: A.I. Is Embedded in Your Election Experience. So Are Its Dangers.
item.description:
The rush to integrate artificial intelligence into major social media platforms has placed a slew of potential pitfalls between voters and reliable information about elections, dangers that tech companies are addressing inconsistently, if at all.

Ahead of the midterms next month, chatbots, media generation services and automated content moderation systems are increasingly shaping voter choices, according to political experts and new research, even as A.I. enables new forms of toxic content.

A.I. tools, some introduced just months before the election, have contributed to biased and inaccurate information about the polls and amplified foreign influence operations. They have also elevated low-quality slop content, which is now tainting the training data that informs chatbot responses, according to researchers.

And despite pressuring tech companies for details about testing, safeguards and the extent of voter interactions with A.I., lawmakers and watchdog groups have said that the companies are not sharing enough information about those efforts.

“We’re in uncharted territory at this point,” said Deen Freelon, a professor of communication at the University of Pennsylvania who studies digital politics.

More than in any other election, tech companies are injecting A.I. into all levels of the user experience. During the last national election in 2024, platforms were offering basic A.I. image generation tools. Those have bloomed in 2026 into advanced services combining audio, video and image capabilities.

Curious about a candidate’s policies? Google delivers an A.I. overview before showing the politician’s website in search results. Scrolling social media? Prepare to see attack ads with fabricated images of candidates.

One in five voters plan to use A.I. to look into a race on their ballot, according to a survey released this month by the American Association of Political Consultants Foundation. Twice that number have already received election details through an A.I. search summary.

And yet just 1 percent of the polled voters considered A.I. to be their most credible source for election information, the survey found.

“This is the first election where A.I. is deeply embedded into the platforms,” said Max Read, the U.S. director of civic innovation at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a research organization.

The institute has been reviewing efforts by major social media platforms to protect political discourse, election integrity and public safety. On Thursday, researchers released a report with their conclusion: Transparency and human oversight are lagging A.I.’s breakneck development pace. Social media platforms are relying on a hodgepodge of A.I. policies, resulting in “meaningful gaps” in how artificially generated content is disclosed or restricted ahead of the midterms, the report found.

Platforms are also increasingly turning to automated and crowdsourced options over humans to moderate content, although the extent remained a mystery to the institute’s researchers. Relying on A.I. for such work is a gamble for companies trying to account for context and nuance during fast-moving, intensive events like elections, the researchers said.

“Their response has been uneven, poorly documented and, in several cases, poorly suited to addressing the harms it is meant to prevent,” Mr. Read said.

Tech companies are facing increasing political pressure to clarify how A.I. plays into their policies for handling election-related disinformation. Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla, both Democrats from California, wrote last month to the heads of companies including Google, Meta, Snap, TikTok and xAI asking for details about their plans to defend election integrity and combat false narratives during the midterms.

Google offered the most extensive answers about A.I., including that it would use the technology in its search features to connect users to vetted information about polling locations, registration deadlines and real-time voting results. But the senators said in statements that the companies’ replies as a whole were inconsistent and incomplete, especially so close to the midterms.

“Social media companies hold enormous power over the content voters see: They decide what to amplify and what not to,” Mr. Schiff said.

In a blog post earlier this month, TikTok laid out its midterms strategy, which included labeling A.I.-generated content and allowing U.S. users to add context to posts through its Footnotes feature. The company said in a separate statement that it was “dedicated to maintaining a safe and secure platform.”

Google said in a statement that it rigorously tests its A.I. overviews for accuracy and also helps users identify A.I. content through prominent labels on YouTube, watermarks and disclosures on election ads. Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, responded that it has robust election safety plans, including real-time threat modeling. The company said it thoroughly tests its A.I. models to ward off wrong answers about the elections.

Most major tech companies are making an effort to preserve election integrity, according to Democracy Works, a nonpartisan organization that is partnering this year with most of the major chatbot developers to share verified election information. XAI is the exception; it also did not reply substantively to Senators Padilla and Schiff.

The acceleration of A.I. technology, and the occasional tendency of chatbots to veer away from neutral facts, makes their work difficult, said Luis Lozada, the chief executive of Democracy Works.

“I don’t think they’re just completely negligent,” he said. “I just think that this is a very, very difficult issue to navigate.”

This summer, the Brennan Center for Justice, a voting rights and democracy group, found that the most popular chatbots regularly pushed back against false election narratives. The A.I., however, could also be prompted to generate content that could undermine elections, such as images of people stuffing multiple ballots.

OpenAI has modified its tools in response to those findings, according to both the company and Brennan. Instead of generating seemingly realistic images of voter fraud, it now renders them as cartoons in an attempt to block intentionally deceptive content without curtailing freedom of speech.

“We are degrading the evidentiary value of an image while still allowing social commentary,” said Josh Lawson, the head of civic and strategic risk at OpenAI. It is one of numerous efforts the company has taken, he said, to screen out malicious attempts to undermine the elections.

In October, Brennan researchers conducted a new round of tests. Only OpenAI had tightened its controls over election falsehoods, they found in a new analysis published on Thursday. Other chatbots from Google, Meta and others had regressed.

(The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Chatbots have become yet another source of information that can be exploited for influence campaigns. The most popular models now sometimes cite known sources of politically biased content or foreign disinformation, including news sites fabricated by or mimicked by Kremlin-linked propaganda operations, according to disinformation researchers.

VisionHeight, a cybersecurity company, reported this month that it found a network of 37 A.I.-filled sites purporting to provide state or regional news that were created in a single day by an anonymous organization in September. The sites also included code that effectively welcomed the A.I. tools that “crawl” for the content that powers chatbots.

The sites fed the chatbots information about candidates in 11 House races in seven states, most of them Democrats.

“The sites are not written for voters,” VisionHeight’s report said. “They are written for the A.I. systems voters ask.”

NewsGuard, a company monitoring harmful online content, has identified more than 1,100 such organizations. It defines them as “pink slime,” sites that “present themselves as professional news outlets but are secretly backed by partisan groups.”

In its own tests, NewsGuard found that chatbots, when prompted about narratives that appear in these partisan sites, cited them nearly half the time.

In some cases, Russia has managed to successfully inject its state propaganda, including about American politics, into chatbots’ training data, according to NewsGuard and other researchers.

When Alethea, a company that tracks influence operations, asked about disinformation long circulated by the Kremlin, some of the most prominent chatbots mentioned Russian state propaganda sources and fabricated news outlets.

XAI’s Grok, for example, was asked about the impact of a European ban on Russian natural gas. It referenced InfoRos, an arm of the Russian military intelligence agency that the United States cited for trying to interfere in the 2020 American presidential election.

“When you use a chatbot,” said Lisa Kaplan, Alethea’s founder, “you are not expecting to be deceived by a foreign actor who’s trying to manipulate you.”

item.title: Mortgage Rates Remain Above 7%, Pushing Home Prices Lower in Some Areas
item.description:
Elevated mortgage rates and high home prices have pushed many potential buyers to the sidelines, crimping home sales and prompting housing experts to lower their recovery forecasts for the rest of the year.

The mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac said Thursday that the most popular home loan in the United States — the 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage — slipped to 7.32 percent, the fifth consecutive week that rates have been above 7 percent.

High housing costs have put the market in a deep freeze, but prices are falling in some pockets of the country.

“What we’re seeing is more motivated sellers that are cutting prices,” said Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor.com, a listings website.

Prices on more than 20 percent of listings were reduced September, said Mr. Berner. Some markets that soared during the pandemic are correcting, he added, pointing to cities in Florida and Texas. “What were the hot markets are now the pretty cool markets,” he said.

In Austin, for example, home prices slid more than 8 percent in September from a year earlier, according to a report from Realtor.com, using a metric called price per square foot, which is used to calculate the value of a property relative to its size.

Buyers are more educated now and have more flexibility to wait, said Crystal Olenbush, a real estate agent in Austin. Sellers, on the other hand, are feeling pressure to price their homes more realistically, she said, adding that she is seeing more reductions as the market resets.

“People are negotiating,” she said. “They are getting all kinds of opportunities.”

Still, affordability remains an issue nationwide. The median sales price of U.S. homes rose 1.3 percent in September from a year earlier, to $417,500, the 39th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases, according to a report released last week by the National Association of Realtors, a trade group.

Prices began to surge during the pandemic, when mortgage rates fell below 3 percent. As the housing market began to heat up, bidding wars broke out, which pushed up home prices around the country.

Since then, homeowners have been unwilling to move, which would mean trading their ultralow rates for higher ones. That created a lock-in effect that has helped keep prices elevated, said Lu Liu, an assistant professor of finance at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania.

“There could be a behavioral story where people are not willing to take a loss,” she said. “It really depends on whether you’re willing to bite the bullet.”

The higher housing costs have hammered existing-home sales, which fell 2.2 percent in September from the year before, NAR reported. Other key real estate metrics — housing starts, pending home sales and builder confidence — have all slumped recently.

Experts point to elevated inflation as an underlying problem. Higher energy costs are driving inflation higher as the war in Iran chokes the world’s supply of crude oil. Consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher in September than a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. But wages have been relatively flat.

“One of the biggest challenges we’re facing right now, especially for first-time home buyers, is that wage growth is not outpacing inflation,” Mr. Berner said.

The sluggishness is prompting experts to revise their forecasts for a housing market recovery. “We expect housing activity to improve around the end of 2027, when we look for mortgage rates to decline,” analysts at Oxford Economics wrote Tuesday in a research note.

Until then, they added, “we think housing activity will be more characterized by gridlock.”

Despite the market downturn, a bright spot has emerged for buyers. Sellers are now reconsidering market conditions, which can give buyers the upper hand.

“The market is clearly tilting in favor of buyers able to negotiate better prices,” Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist, said last week on a call with reporters.

And builders of new homes are more willing to negotiate to clear inventory.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share since 2020, according to a survey released Monday by the National Association of Home Builders, a trade group.

The average price cut was 6 percent for the seventh consecutive month, the group said. In addition, 65 percent of builders reported using sales incentives in October, the 19th straight month that at least 60 percent of builders have done so.

“Our research shows that new home buyers, who often take advantage of reduced rate offerings from builders, pay as much as a full percentage point less on their mortgage.” Mr. Berner said in a report last year. “New construction should absolutely be on the radar of any prospective home buyer.”
